modes.cue_notes: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Let both knees fall to one side, allowing a gentle spinal rotation. Hold each side. Can also be done dynamically (sweeping knees side to side) as a transition or warm-up. For yin, hold each side passively and let the weight of the legs create the rotation.

source: Traditional yin yoga; see Paul Grilley, Bernie Clark, Sarah Powers
notes: A gentle lateral spinal rotation targeting the outer hip and IT band. The gallbladder meridian runs along the lateral body. Often used as a transition pose between supine postures or after deeper hip openers.

breathing_cues.entering: Exhale to let the knees fall to one side: the exhale is what releases the rotation; avoid using muscular effort to push the knees down.
breathing_cues.holding: Each inhale gently lifts the ribs and creates a small counter-rotation in the thorax; each exhale allows the lumbar and sacral region to soften deeper into the twist. Notice the space between each vertebra opening.
breathing_cues.exiting: Inhale the knees back to center on the breath, use the core rather than momentum, then exhale and allow them to fall to the opposite side.

modifications.name: Feet wider apart
modifications.description: Place feet wider than hips before letting the knees fall, reducing the intensity of the hip rotation and making the pose more accessible for sensitive SI joints.

modifications.name: Bolster between knees
modifications.description: Place a bolster or folded blanket between the thighs before dropping to one side, creating a supported version that reduces the range of lumbar rotation.

modifications.name: Dynamic sweeping
modifications.description: Use the pose dynamically, sweep knees from side to side with the breath, as a warming or transitional movement rather than a static yin hold.

modifications.name: Hand guidance
modifications.description: Use the opposite hand to gently guide the top knee toward the floor, adding a small amount of assisted depth for students who want more intensity in the outer hip.

emotional_release_potential.notes: The gallbladder meridian governs decision-making and indecision; lateral spinal rotation releases holding patterns in the lumbar and sacrum associated with chronic stress and over-control.
The fluid, yielding quality of this pose, letting the legs drop by their own weight, teaches the nervous system to trust surrender over control, a key theme of wood-element work.
